title: Memory store eviction + prefix correlation — long-context triage
topics: batching effects on cache hit rate
summary: SE triage with Hyperion experienced intermittent QoS regressions when running long-context conversational workloads. Root causes explored: eviction thresholds, prefix reuse causing apparent cache thrash, SSD paging latencies under burst, and quantization-induced changes to memory layout. Agreed to run controlled experiments and capture KV diagnostics, disk metrics, and per-batch hit/miss breakdowns.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Location: Zoom
Record link: (redacted)
Attendees: Diego (Redwood AE), Sophie (Redwood SE), Ravi (Redwood Solutions), Maya (Hyperion ML), Tom (Platform), Priya (AI Ops)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Customer sees sudden latency spikes and quality regressions on long-context chat flows.
- Symptoms: high tail latency, model responses truncated mid-sentence, token drops when context > ~12k and with repeated prompt prefixes.
- Suspected drivers: KV eviction and paging interplay, prefix reuse causing KV addresses to be churned, heavy batching reducing effective cache locality.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Diego: All right, hey everyone thanks for carving out the time. The goal is to go deep on the KV behavior you observed — eviction/paging and how prefix reuse might be interacting. Sophie will lead the debugging.

[00:22] Sophie: Hi hi, can folks mute other devices — okay. Maya, can you briefly describe the repro pattern? You mentioned it happens more when you run long multi-turn sessions with the same intro prompt.

[00:34] Maya: Yeah so we have a clinical assistant that holds ~20k token histories. It's a structured prompt with a patient summary block at the top — that block is identical across many conversations (prefix reuse), then conversation-specific tokens append. With that we see occasional 99th-percentile token latency jump and sometimes the response drops to half a reply, like generation gets cut off.

[00:58] Tom: To add, we've been running on dedicated nodes, 8xA100-style, with NVMe scratch attached inside the VPC. We noticed the disk queue depth spikes aligned with the latency events.

[01:17] Sophie: Okay that's great detail. A couple immediate hypotheses: 1) prefix reuse causing the same KV keys but different token positions leading to inefficient shard placement or collisions; 2) eviction threshold is too aggressive (max_kv_percent ring is low) so long contexts cause thrash and pages are spilling to NVMe; 3) batching increases the working set concurrently so momentary memory pressure forces paging.

[01:49] Priya: Quick question — are these nodes using SSD paging (i.e., runtime spills KV to disk) or is it purely in-memory in your private deployment?

[02:02] Sophie: You're on Redwood Dedicated, correct? For Dedicated we do allow KV spillover to local NVMe if memory high-water hits. There's a configurable 'eviction_threshold' and 'prefetch_window' parameter. Also there's the 'kv_shard_map' which controls how token KV is sharded across GPUs — misaligned sharding with repeated prefixes can make locality worse.

[02:32] Ravi: One nuance — quantization also affects this. Lower-bit quantization can change memory layout and (in some cases) increase per-token metadata, which changes the eviction calculus. Have you rolled any quantized variants for the same model?

[02:51] Maya: We ran int8 last week as an experiment. The timing of the regressions aligned with that rollout but we rolled it back and still saw some issues. So maybe quantization changed the profile and left some residual behavior.

[03:07] Sophie: Right, rolling back binary doesn't always reset eviction history — there's warm state. But the main thing we'll need is a timeline-correlated kvstats dump around the event.

[03:18] Tom: We captured some log snippets. When the spike happened we saw lines like "evicting shard 3 reason mem_pressure" and "paging kv page id 0x7a6 to /dev/nvme0n1p1". The timestamps line up with the high tail latency in our app logs.

[03:41] Sophie: That's strong evidence of NVMe paging during the event. Two things to check: NVMe latency distribution (p95/p99) and whether the NVMe controller is being saturated by other system activity. Also kernel page cache and droppage — if you mount disk with noop scheduler it might affect latency.

[03:58] Priya: We're on a shared VPC subnet; there's burst traffic from other tenants sometimes — could that cause the NVMe stalls?

[04:08] Sophie: If you're on multi-tenant VPC with EBS-backed NVMe, noisy neighbors can absolutely impact tail IO. For private on-prem with direct-attached NVMe we usually get more stable latency.

[04:25] Diego: I want to come back to prefix reuse. Maya, you said the patient summary block is identical across many sessions — do you tokenize it the same way every time? Any whitespace changes?

[04:37] Maya: It's templated, so identical characters mostly. We do sanitize whitespace but there are occasional punctuation differences depending on clinician-entered notes.

[04:48] Sophie: Even small differences change tokenization boundaries and could produce different KV keys. If you have a high fraction of exact-match prefixes, it's usually good for cache hits; however if they're near-identical but differ in one token, you end up with a large number of similar keys which can cause conflict in our shard hashing scheme and accelerate eviction for neighbors.

[05:12] Ravi: Another thing — when the runtime decides to prefetch, it walks forward a 'prefetch_window' of tokens to warm the KV. If your conversation patterns alternate between a few high-frequency prefixes and lots of unique tails, prefetch can pollute cache with tails and push useful prefix entries out. That's an anti-locality effect.

[05:33] Tom: So prefetching is sometimes bad. Can we tune it down?

[05:36] Sophie: Yes, prefetch_window is tunable. There's also 'prefetch_policy' that can be 'aggressive', 'balanced', or 'minimal'. For workloads with heavy prefix reuse, 'minimal' often helps.

[05:48] [06:00] Maya: What about eviction policy? Are we using LRU? LFU? Something custom?

[06:06] Sophie: The runtime uses an adaptive hybrid — it's LRU-ish but with shard-aware weights; we call it adaptive recency-frequency. In practice, you can expose two knobs: 'eviction_threshold' (percent of reserved KV memory to start evicting) and 'eviction_batch' which controls how many entries get evicted per cycle. If the threshold is too low and eviction_batch is large, you get aggressive churn.

[06:31] Diego: Also note the shard packing heuristics — when a shard fills, it may move to a different GPU or trigger spillover. That movement can look like eviction but is really a rebalance. Those events should have logs showing 'shard_migrate' vs 'evict'.

[06:47] Tom: Our logs show both evict and migrate. Could migrations cause transient extra IO?

[06:54] Sophie: Yes, when migrating we snapshot pages and transfer them across PCIe/NIC; if migration chooses disk as intermediate, you'll see more disk IO. We should confirm migration vs evict counts.

[07:08] Maya: Is there a utility you recommend to capture per-token hit/miss?

[07:12] Sophie: We have 'kvprobe' (internal/debug) that can produce per-request hit/miss traces and a heatmap, plus 'kvstats' which aggregates per-shard counters. If you can run kvprobe on a repro run that will be extremely helpful.

[07:25] Priya: Is kvprobe safe in production?

[07:28] Sophie: It's read-only and sampling by default. We won't alter state; just get snapshots and counters. We'll provide a config that samples at 1% to minimize overhead.

[07:38] [08:00] Ravi: Another subtlety: quantization can change cache address alignment if we pack multiple 4-bit items into a 32-bit word, which alters which tokens share a cache line. That can increase evictions if alignment crosses hot/cold boundaries. It sounds obscure but it's happened.

[08:17] Maya: Hmm we did int8, not 4-bit, but still — interesting.

[08:23] Sophie: Also consider the batching factor. You mentioned running high batch sizes to maximize throughput. Bigger batches mean simultaneous KV access to different ranges which widens the working set. That reduces per-request locality and can drop hit rates.

[08:40] Tom: We have auto-batching set to 128 tokens/req and a batch size cap of 64. Should we lower that?

[08:47] Sophie: For long-context, try lowering max batch concurrency or reducing max tokens per request if latency/cold-hit matters more than throughput. Alternatively we can enable prefix-aware batching where requests with identical leading prefixes are grouped to improve locality — that requires a small routing hook. We can provide a reference implementation.

[09:12] Maya: That prefix-aware batching sounds promising. Do you have an example?

[09:18] Sophie: We'll share a snippet. It's basically a hash of the first N tokens as a routing key, then the router attempts to co-schedule similar keys on the same GPU to preserve cache locality. Caveat: it can increase head-of-line blocking if not tuned.

[09:35] [10:00] Priya: On the VPC side, if NVMe IO is variable, could we switch to RAM-backed tmpfs for paging?

[10:07] Sophie: tmpfs will use system RAM so it defeats the purpose — you'd need more RAM than your working set. If you have excess ephemeral RAM you could use it as a fast backing store but typically you want persistent NVMe. On-prem direct-attached NVMe with consistent firmware is ideal.

[10:23] Tom: Any kernel-level flags we should tune? Readahead? I/O scheduler?

[10:27] Sophie: Yes, set I/O scheduler to 'none' for NVMe, reduce readahead if synchronous small IO is common, and tune the NVMe driver to reduce queue depth if you see contention. Also check for CPU steal in the host and NUMA misbinding — if NUMA causes a thread to access remote memory, you'll see latency increases.

[10:45] Maya: Can we run a micro-benchmark to confirm that the problem is disk latency + eviction rather than model kernel slowness?

[10:51] Sophie: Absolutely. Proposed micro-bench: 1) synthetic sequence generator with repeating prefixes, 2) run at production concurrency and collect kvstats + iostat + nvme-cli latency, 3) toggle prefetch/prefetch_window and measure p95/p99 and hit/miss rates. We'll provide the harness.

[11:14] Ravi: Also capture per-batch serialization time inside the runtime, because sometimes CPU-side serialization of KV entries becomes a bottleneck under heavy batching and looks like disk latency.

[11:26] Tom: Good call. We'll add host-level perf counters.

[11:30] [12:00] Diego: A quick operational mitigation: raise eviction_threshold temporarily during peak loads to avoid spilling. That trades memory headroom for avoiding NVMe penalty. But be careful — raising too high risks OOM.

[12:12] Sophie: And reduce prefetch_window to keep tails from polluting. Combine with prefix-aware batching and you may see immediate improvements.

[12:21] Maya: If we tune those, do you expect the quality truncation to stop? The truncation seems like the generator stops when context can't be accessed fast enough.

[12:29] Sophie: Likely yes — when KV fetch latency spikes the generation loop misses deadlines and may cut off. Keeping KV in RAM or avoiding paging should restore continuity.

[12:40] Tom: Anything to watch with quantization if we re-roll int8?

[12:44] Sophie: Re-run the eviction-related tests under int8. If you see more churn, try smaller quantization steps or alternative packing. We'll give guidance.

[12:54] [13:00] Maya: For the immediate next step, we'll share the prompt set and run the kvprobe with Sophie’s config.

[13:06] Diego: Great. We'll also prepare a tuning doc showing example values for prefetch_window, eviction_threshold, and batch limits for similar workload patterns.

[13:15] Priya: One more question — are there known bugs around shard migration and lock contention in the runtime version we're on? We are on 1.8.2-rc.

[13:27] Sophie: There was a tweak in 1.8.3 that changed migration pacing to reduce disk writes — it may help. We'll check release notes and recommend patching to the stable 1.8.4 where a migration deadlock was fixed. We'll include that in the follow-up.

[13:42] [14:00] Tom: OK. To summarize (Tom): we'll run a repro with kvprobe and disk metrics; Redwood to provide tuning knobs and a prefix-aware batching example; both sides to coordinate a controlled test next week.

[14:15] Diego: Yep, and Sophie will analyze eviction/paging traces and advise on temporary mitigation (raise threshold) vs long-term fix (router + patch).

[14:26] Sophie: I'll also check if there's any instrumentation we can add to surface 'hot prefix set' in the console so you can see which prefixes consume the most KV. That might help prioritize rewriting templates to reduce near-duplicates.

[14:40] Maya: Thanks, that would be very helpful.

[14:44] Diego: Any final items?

[14:47] Priya: No. Thanks everyone.

[14:50] Diego: Cool — we'll follow up with the artifact links and schedule.

[14:55] End of recording.
